name: Precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex)
summary: The gyrus immediately in front of the central sulcus, extending over the vertex onto the medial surface as the anterior part of the paracentral lobule. Its layer V giant pyramidal (Betz) cells and many smaller pyramidal neurons give rise to the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts. The body is mapped upside down and distorted along it (the motor homunculus): the leg and foot on the medial surface, the trunk and arm over the convexity with a disproportionately large hand area at the hand knob, and the face and tongue lowest, just above the Sylvian fissure. Because the ACA supplies the leg area and the MCA the rest, the pattern of weakness after a stroke tells you which artery is involved.

anatomy.location: Between the precentral sulcus in front and the central sulcus behind, from the lateral sulcus to the superior margin and onto the medial surface; recognized on axial MRI by the omega-shaped hand knob and by the thicker cortex compared with the postcentral gyrus.

subdivisions.name: Medial (paracentral) part
subdivisions.note: leg, foot and perineum; ACA territory

subdivisions.name: Hand knob
subdivisions.note: hand and fingers, the largest representation

subdivisions.name: Inferior part
subdivisions.note: face, tongue, larynx; MCA superior division

function: Execution of voluntary skilled movement of the contralateral body through the corticospinal tract and of the face through the corticobulbar tract; force and direction coding of movement.

bestView.label: hand knob of the precentral gyrus, in front of the central sulcus
precentral gyrus with the central sulcus behind
paracentral lobule: leg area on the medial surface

imaging.normalAppearance: Identify the central sulcus on axial images by the hand knob (an inverted omega) on the precentral gyrus and by the pars marginalis of the cingulate sulcus on the medial surface; the precentral cortex is thicker and slightly darker on T2 than the postcentral cortex. Functional MRI and tractography map the tract for surgical planning.

pathology.finding: Ribbon of restricted diffusion along the precentral gyrus; an isolated hand-knob infarct causes pure hand weakness mimicking a peripheral nerve lesion.
Enhancing dural mass at the vertex compressing the paracentral lobule with contralateral (or bilateral) leg weakness and focal seizures.
T2 hyperintensity along the corticospinal tract and T2*/SWI hypointensity of the precentral cortex from iron.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; T1+Gd for masses; fMRI/tractography for surgery

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral weakness with the pattern of the homunculus: face and arm (lateral lesion) or leg (medial lesion)
Loss of fine finger movements out of proportion to power
lesionEffects.mechanism: Corticospinal control of independent finger movement

lesionEffects.deficit: Focal motor (Jacksonian) seizures marching along the homunculus
Initial flaccidity then spasticity and hyperreflexia

examination: Pronator drift, finger tapping and rapid alternating movements
Compare leg with arm weakness to infer ACA versus MCA
Ask about focal twitching or marching seizures
pearls: Isolated hand weakness of sudden onset is a hand-knob cortical infarct until proven otherwise, not a radial or ulnar palsy
Weakness in the leg alone: paracentral lobule (ACA), spinal cord or a parasagittal mass
